analysis.one_liner: Lets students sue colleges in court instead of being forced into arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would bar colleges that take federal aid from forcing students into arbitration, was introduced by a House Democrat with 4 cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many colleges require students to sign arbitration agreements and class-action waivers when they enroll, meaning disputes about fraud, discrimination, or billing must be settled in a private process run by a firm the college effectively selects, with no judge and no appeal. This bill would make those agreements unenforceable for any college that participates in federal student aid, and would amend the Higher Education Act to prohibit colleges from restricting students' ability to bring claims in court, individually or in groups. It would take effect one year after enactment. The bill was referred to the Education and Labor and Judiciary committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future students at colleges that participate in federal aid programs, especially those with fraud, discrimination, or billing disputes against their school. The roughly 90% of students who enroll under agreements that waive their right to sue would regain access to a public courtroom, a jury, and class actions where individual claims are too small to litigate alone.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make chapter 1 of title 9 of the U.S. Code — the federal law requiring courts to enforce arbitration agreements — inapplicable to enrollment agreements between students and institutions of higher education.

It would amend the Higher Education Act to bar participating colleges from requiring or enforcing any limitation on students' ability to pursue claims in court, including restrictions on choice of law, jury trials, or venue.
Because it conditions the rule on participation in federal student aid, the restriction would reach essentially every accredited college, since few operate without federal aid money.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities that currently use mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers would lose that shield and face the risk of jury trials and class actions. Institutions with weak legal exposure — often for-profit schools — would bear the largest change in liability. Some of that cost could be passed to students through legal fees or tuition, and schools would lose a dispute process that is often cheaper and faster for small claims.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is not always worse for students: it can be faster and cheaper for individual disputes than a multi-year court case, and schools could argue that losing it raises costs that show up in tuition or legal expenses.

The bill removes colleges' flexibility to design their own dispute-resolution processes and applies a single federal rule to every institution that takes federal aid, from large public universities to small private colleges.

The narrower ability to pursue claims might encourage more litigation against schools, and critics of limiting arbitration generally argue it invites class actions that can extract large fees while delivering little to class members.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — restoring students' access to courts and class actions against the very institutions they paid for a degree — is substantial, particularly against schools accused of fraud or misconduct. The main honest cost is that arbitration can serve small individual claims efficiently, and pushing all disputes into court could raise institutions' legal costs. On balance the bill targets a well-documented imbalance: it would govern institutions that receive federal funds and that students cannot negotiate with as a condition of enrollment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee — referred first to a House Judiciary subcommittee and never scheduled for a hearing, markup, or floor vote — until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Maxine Waters introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, with Mark Takano, Jackie Speier, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Steve Cohen as the original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Education and Labor Committee and, in addition, to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
On April 8, 2019, it was referred to the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee vote, a hearing, or a floor vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and universities that require students to sign away their right to sue keep that practice, since the rule was never enacted. Students' claims against their schools remain in private arbitration.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges that require arbitration kept the practice

for.name: Mark Takano, Jackie Speier, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 28, 2019 and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and its Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Accepted the referral, assigned it to the subcommittee on April 8, 2019, and never scheduled a markup or reported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape is unknown; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, and no committee or floor action occurred.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities that take federal student aid
industries.note: These institutions currently can require students to sign arbitration agreements and class-action waivers as a condition of enrollment, insulating them from jury trials and group lawsuits. The bill would strip that protection from any school participating in federal aid.

The bill removes college enrollment agreements from the universe of contracts that federal law obligates courts to enforce through arbitration, shrinking the private market in resolving student-school disputes.
